content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper presents a group-equivariant transformer architecture on images with group convolutions instead of group equivariant attention. In comparison to previously known group-equivariant attention networks, it removes attention over the rotation group and replacing it by full spatial attention. To keep expressiveness, the architecture utilizes group convolution instead of point-wise MLPs. Further, APS is utilized to keep equivariance during subsampling. The presented architecture is evaluated on rotMNIST and CIFAR10.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- The paper is well written
- The paper presents exhaustive ablations studies for all presented architecture modifications.
- It is interesting to see that group invariant positional encoding seem to be not needed.
- The presented architecture clearly outperforms the baseline on the benchmark datasets.
- The math and group formalisms are sound.

Weaknesses:
- It does not become clear to me why the group equivariant convolutions should act as an implicit positional encoding, as stated by the authors. The experiments only show that the accuracy is better but that might have different reasons.
- Similarly, Section 4.2 states "As a result, the group-equivariant convolution stem greatly enhances the representation power of the network". This is not really shown by theory or experiments. It is only shown that classification accuracy goes up.
- The paper seems to present only a slightly modified architecture in comparison to previous work. The modifications seem to boil down to 1) removing the main aspect (equivariant positional encodings/attention) from the baseline, replacing it with a variant closer to standard multi-head attention, 2) introducing G-CNNs from existing work, and 3) utilizing APS subsampling from existing work. In total, the conceptual contribution is limited.
- I am skeptical if the evaluated tasks are substitutes for an actually relevant problem. They are good proof of concept datasets in cases where novel theoretical concepts are introduced, which is, however, not the case here. If the goal in this work is to tune the architecture, I would at least expect evaluations on larger datasets.
- Usually in works about equivariant architectures, the methods are evaluated in different example rotation scenarios, such as AR/AR, NR/AR, NR/NR (augmented rotation / not rotated). This is only partially done here and not sufficiently explained (see below). To me, the experiments are inconclusive due to that.
- The paper spends a lot of space introducing formalisms from previous work but then does not really use them to introduce something new.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity:
- The paper suffers a bit from too many individual modules and too similar acronyms, making it hard to follow in some parts
- Cifar10+ is never cited or explained in the paper. I have to guess that it includes randomly rotated examples during training.
- It does also not become clear if the CIFAR10 test examples are rotated or not. If not, then the architecture is mostly evaluated in non rotated scenarios, which seems odd to me.

The novelty of the work is limited. The individual parts are mostly from existing works, only the joint architecture is novel.

The paper quality is good.

The method is quite complicated and will be hard to reproduce without published code.
content.summary_of_the_review:
In summary, I tend to vote for rejecting this paper due to the above reasons. The main concern is the missing novelty. Also, the evaluation / theory fails to conclusively support the statements made by the authors.

Minors:
- Figure 2 b) one red square is wrong
- Table 5 and Table 6 should include references
- The text is missing articles at some places

content.comment: Thank you for the constructive comments. We will revise our paper by reflecting on the comments and resubmit it to another venue. We answer some questions you asked as follows: As demonstrated in previous work (Islam et al., 2020), convolution with zero padding can learn implicit positional information by using zero padding as an anchor. In Tab. 2, we demonstrate that fixed group-equivariant convolution with zero padding, which means that it does not learn local patterns, outperforms the model with no positional encoding, proving that group-equivariant convolution also functions as implicit positional encoding. We will move the preliminary and basic concept introduction to the appendix and add the experimental information you suggested. To demonstrate the generalizability of the proposed equivariant networks, studies on group equivariance frequently conduct experiments on datasets where group equivariance is undesirable.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The authors propose a group-equivariant architecture for image transformers by replacing the fully connected feed-forward networks in the layers by group-equivalent convolution networks, adding an group-equivariant subsampler at the end of each layer, and using a group-equivariant convolutional lifting of the input, replacing the positional embedding. This leads to a simpler architecture than the group-equivariant self-attention proposed by Romero and Cordonnier. 

They conduct a number of experiments to justify their architectural decision (choice of the subsampler, removing the positional embedding). 

On two popular baselines (rotated Mnist and CIFAR-10), they compare their model with group equivariant self attention models, and two implementation of group-equivariant CNN (Cohen and Weiler). The model achieves state of the art on both datasets.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strengths**

The architecture proposed is an interesting replacement for group-equivariant self-attention, and achieves better performance on the test sets. The ablations and experiments are compelling.

**Weaknesses**

The model proposed fills the performance gap between GSA-Nets and group-equivariant CNN. On the other hand, the new architecture only offers marginal performance improvements over group-equivariant CNN. 

The architecture proposed is very close to group-equivariant CNN. In fact, it is a multilayer GE CNN with a few self-attention layers. The experiments seem to suggest that the benefit of the self-attention layers is very limited.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is clearly written, the architecture is original and the model and experiment are clearly described, allowing for reproducibility.
content.summary_of_the_review: The architecture proposed is interesting, and solves the performance problem of previous group-equivariant transformers. However, the resulting model is very close to a GE CNN, and the benefits of adding self-attention layers is not clear to me.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a new Group-Equivariant Transformer called CGTR. The authors motivate the approach by claiming that exact group invariant positional encoding is not needed and is computationally expensive. Instead, the authors introduce a group convolutional feedforward network that is equivariant and learns the invariant positional encoding. Other changes include a group equivariant convolutional stem that is used for lifting and group equivariant pooling. Experiments are conducted on standard benchmarks including Rotation MNIST and CIFAR10 for the group $p4m$.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The overall motivation for this paper is clear and interesting. The figures while a bit confusing are a nice addition to ease the exposition of this paper. However, I have several questions and concerns that I list below:

 - How is the lifting to the group performed in eqn 3? In Kondor & Trevidi 2018 [1] this was clear but this is not specified here.
 - The overall writing is not sufficiently polished. For example, in section 3 felt like the an original contribution and not enough was done to delineate that this was not actually a contribution.
 - Eqn 4 is quite ugly. The inner product accepts 3 things. This is not an inner product, so don't use $\langle, \rangle$ this is an unnecessary abuse of notation.
 - The name group-equivariant convolutional feed-forward network is an oxymoron. If it's a G-CNN then it's not a feedforward (MLP) network. The name just obfuscates things, I recommend changing it.
 - The current approach appears only feasible for discrete subgroups and not continuous groups. This is not made clear enough.
 - S-SA seems like it's just vanilla Self-Attention which is already permutation invariant. Can you comment on the difference between vanilla self-attention and the proposed S-SA if we ignore the group equivariant convolutional network? I'm assuming the main difference could be that the functions are now lifted to the group? Is this correct?
 - Batch Norm is not equivariant by design. So the proposed GCFFN is not equivariant. There are versions of the batch norm that can be made equivariant (Inner Batch Norm[2]) but I suspect the ones used in this paper are not. The same goes for the Swish activation function.
 - The details for how the lifting operation is done in eqn. 9 is not clear. $f$ is a function on the input space but the RHS of eqn 9 is now a function $G$. How do you do this?
 - Something feels off in Tab 1 results. They shouldn't be this bad, with enough parameters on CIFAR10 you should expect higher accuracy. Can you better explain this result? Have you tried training with regularization to prevent some of the overfitting behavior you experience?
 - None of the table numbers have a quantification of uncertainty. This is not good enough for empirical results especially when the numbers are so close for certain tables (e.g. Tab 5). Mean and Standard deviation with p-values are needed.

[1] Kondor, R., & Trivedi, S. (2018, July). On the generalization of equivariance and convolution in neural networks to the action of compact groups. In International Conference on Machine Learning (pp. 2747-2755). PMLR.

[2] https://quva-lab.github.io/e2cnn/_modules/e2cnn/nn/modules/batchnormalization/inner.html
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
** Clarity **
The clarity of the writing could be improved. There are various sections in the paper that are not clear enough. It is not sufficient to claim the equivariance of certain layers. You need to show equivariance. Furthermore, not enough detail is provided about the lifting operation, which appears crucial to the convolutional stem.
- spelling mistakes  for example in section 2.2 "MLPs in the tansformer"
 - some notation is not clear:
 right below Fig.1 what is $\rho^P$? Specifically, what is $P$?

** Quality & Novelty **
The overall novelty of this paper is limited. It is a combination of existing ideas in various other domains. The removal of exact positional encoding is perhaps the most intriguing novelty but what needs to be shown is how the overall Self-Attention + GCFFN are equivariant as a whole not individually. Furthermore, pooling is an invariant operation so I'm confused how equivariance is maintained end-to-end.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall I believe this paper has interesting ideas that could be executed at a higher level. There are presentation issues and I believe certain layers are not equivariant at least it is not immediately clear why they should be equivariant. Due to this limitations my current rating of this paper is a 3.

content.comment: Thank you for the constructive comments. We will revise our paper by reflecting on the comments and resubmit it to another venue. We answer some questions you asked as follows: Sec. 3 is an introduction that, obviously, is not our contribution but rather aims to give readers a better understanding. To avoid confusion, we already cite the GSA-Net (Romero et al., 2020) and use its notation and equation, including Eq. 4. S-SA is nearly identical to standard self-attention except for the feature space defined on group $G$. Inner batch norm (Weiler et al., 2019) is already in use, and swish activation, already used in GSA-Net, is point-wise nonlinearity preserving equivariance, though they were left out for space reasons. On the CIFAR-10 dataset, where rotation equivariance is undesirable, p4-equivariant GSA-Net performs worse despite using regularization to avoid overfitting. We will give the mean, standard deviation, and p-values to remove the uncertainty of the experiments.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper:
This work suggests a new group-equivariant transformer without positional encoding. It largely builds on the former 'GSA-net', but replaces several of its major building blocks. Mainly, it removes the positional encoding all together from the self-attention blocks and instead replaces the linear blocks in the following feed-forward network by group convolutions. This change is shown to preserve group equivariance and so are two additional changes in the architecture - replacing the first (stem) self-attention layer with a group-equivariant convolution and replacing the (max-)pooling layer with 'adaptive polyphase sampling' (APS).
The resulting CGTR is ablated to show individual component contributions and is compared with baseline methods on rotated-MNIST and CIFAR-10, showing relative improvements.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
* The paper proposes several interesting architectural changes in group-equivariant transformers, ones that are able to preserve the group-equivariance, while giving claimed advantages in terms of efficiency and modelling.
* An empirical validation that the proposed changes enable the removal of positional encoding from the self-attention stage.

Weaknesses:
* The contributions of the work seem to be limited, in both theoretical and practical aspects. 
* In terms of the general ideas, the introduction of convolutions into ViTs has been previously shown (e.g. by CvT) to combine the merits of cnn and transformers. Furthermore, the motivation for removing positional encoding is not given, other than making the self-attention fully equivariant (i.e. to any permutation), however positional encoding might still be informative and beneficial in certain settings. There has been works in related domains (e.g. SIREN [neurips 20]) that have found ways to replace positional encodings.
* On the practical side, it is claimed to give 'significant performance gains with less computation and memory'. In terms of computation and memory - there is no specific comparison to other methods (in contrast to e.g. 'Efficient Equivariant Network', neurips 21, which reports FLOPs in addition to parameter counts), hence the impact here is not supported. Also, in terms of the results in general, the improvements do not show new capabilities or strengthening of the general thesis that group-equivariance is an important property of visual transformers. In fact, the experimentation (on CIFAR and MNIST) is limited, even with regard to previous work (like G-SA, which include an additional larger scale data-set)
* To my feeling, the paper is not close to being self-contained or clearly enough explained, for the reader that is not totally familiar with equivariant and convolutional versions of transformers (like myself) to be able to understand the new contributions. I believe that the basic concepts should be better explained, perhaps through example, as found in the relevant baseline papers (e.g. the G-conv and G-SA ones).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: As mentioned above, I think there is room for improvement here. Especially, I find the introduction to be extremely short, listing many references, but not giving the basic background and motivation of using equivariance, which kinds of groups, etc'.
Quality and Novelty: As detailed above, while the work contains some interesting and novel ideas and components, the overall motivation and implications are not clear enough, which harm the quality of the work.
Reproducibility: Sufficient details have been given.
content.summary_of_the_review: As described above, this work potentially contains some novel and interesting developments over current group-equivariant transformers, but they are not well enough motivated and demonstrated in the paper. In addition, I found the text rather difficult to follow, without the constant need to figure out things using the background papers.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper2281 by Reviewer nsqJ

content.title: Response to reviewer nsqJ
content.comment: Thank you for the constructive comments. We will revise our paper by reflecting on the comments and resubmit it to another venue. We answer some questions you asked as follows: Although the GSA-Net (Romero et al., 2020) using group-invariant positional encoding theoretically achieves group equivariance, it requires computation and memory proportional to the bicubic of the order of the group. Large resource requirements prevent GSA-Net from using larger patch sizes. Thus GSA-Net practically adopts local self-attention, limiting the advantage of self-attention, i.e., long-range dependencies modeling. Inspired by these limitations, we replace group-invariant positional encoding with group-equivariant convolution acting as implicit positional encoding and restrict the range of self-attention from the entire group $G$ to just the translation group $T$. As a result, the proposed CGTR closes the performance gap between group-equivariant CNNs and group-equivariant transformers while requiring less computation and memory than GSA-Net. We will include more background and preliminary for a better understanding of the reader. We will clarify our contribution and run additional experiments on larger datasets.
